titre: Human Chromosome 2 Is the Fusion of Two Great Ape Chromosomes
accroche: Humans have 46 chromosomes, great apes 48. The difference comes not from a loss, but from a weld
contenu_vulgarise:
Count the chromosomes of a human being: forty-six. Count those of a chimpanzee, a gorilla, or an orangutan: forty-eight, every time. Two fewer in our species, in every cell, in every individual.

The difference might suggest a loss: two chromosomes vanished along the way. The opposite is what happened: nothing was lost, two chromosomes fused into one.

## A scar readable in the sequence

The end of each chromosome carries a repetitive protective structure, the telomere, always organized in the same direction, like a cap. In 1991, a team led by J.-W. IJdo spots, in the middle of the long human chromosome 2 (not at its end, right in the middle), two series of telomeric repeats joined head to head.

Two protective caps, back to back, inside a single chromosome: this is the signature of a fusion. Two distinct ancestral chromosomes, each with its own ends, were at some point glued together end to end to form just one, carrying their two now-useless telomeres inside the new structure.

A second clue confirms the first. A functional chromosome needs only one centromere, the attachment point that allows it to be distributed during cell division. Human chromosome 2 carries, in addition to its active centromere, the deactivated remains of a second centromere, a little farther along the same arm: exactly what one expects of a chromosome born of two chromosomes, one of whose two centromeres stopped working.

## What the fusion does not change

The fusion made no gene disappear: the two ancestral chromosomes are still there, carried end to end on a single support instead of two. Above all, it shows that the number of chromosomes is in itself a sign of nothing, neither of the quantity of genetic information nor of an organism's complexity. A mouse has forty, a carp more than a hundred, a fern several hundred: the count depends on how the material is packaged, not on what it contains.

The exact date of this fusion remains debated, between several hundred thousand and a few million years ago, but it predates the split between humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans, who all three carry it. What the molecular scar establishes unambiguously, however, is the event itself: two great ape chromosomes, glued together, became one of the twenty-three human chromosomes.

repere.texte: In the middle of human chromosome 2, two series of telomeric repeats are joined head to head: the signature of a fusion between two distinct ancestral chromosomes, each originally equipped with its own ends.
repere.source: IJdo, Baldini, Ward, Reeders & Wells, “Origin of human chromosome 2: an ancestral telomere-telomere fusion,” PNAS, 88, 1991

carte.punch: Two great ape chromosomes, glued end to end, became a single human chromosome.
carte.idee: Humans have 46 chromosomes, great apes 48. The difference does not come from a loss of genetic material: two ancestral chromosomes fused end to end to form human chromosome 2, which still carries the scar of this fusion in its sequence.

quiz.question: What does the presence, in the middle of human chromosome 2, of two series of telomeric repeats joined head to head indicate?
choix: That this chromosome lost part of its genetic material over the course of evolution
That two distinct ancestral chromosomes fused to form this single chromosome
That this chromosome repairs itself more often than the others after a break
That this chromosome never had a functional centromere
quiz.explication: Telomeres normally protect the end of a chromosome; finding two back to back in the middle of chromosome 2 is the signature of a fusion between two distinct chromosomes, confirmed by the presence of a deactivated second centromere in the same place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides the joined telomeres, which second clue confirms that human chromosome 2 results from a fusion?
choix: It carries the deactivated remains of a second centromere, in addition to its active centromere
It contains twice as many genes as the other human chromosomes
It is about twice as long as all the other human chromosomes
It never completely divides during meiosis
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card states that chromosome 2 carries, in addition to its active centromere, the deactivated remains of a second centromere, exactly what one expects from the fusion of two chromosomes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the chromosome 2 fusion show, according to the card, about a species' number of chromosomes?
choix: It directly determines the size of a species' genome
It makes it possible to predict an organism's life expectancy
It is in itself a sign of neither the quantity of genetic information nor an organism's complexity
It is always even in mammals, odd in other species
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card concludes that the fusion made no gene disappear: the number of chromosomes depends on how the material is packaged, not on what it contains.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before which event in human evolution does the chromosome 2 fusion come, according to the card?
choix: The appearance of articulate language in Homo sapiens
The split between humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans
The domestication of the dog by human populations
The first Homo sapiens leaving Africa
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card places the fusion before the split between humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans, who all three carry this same chromosomal scar.
